setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. The team is switching from the old way of keeping {record|the} to a new version of {system|the}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you have to start using a new version of {system|the} for {record|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says nobody will check whether you actually use the new system.
The switch is happening during a busy week.
detail: The new screens use a different color scheme.
Most of the team is new to it too.

tiers.1: A new requirement affects every entry, so it comes first.
tiers.2: Feedback on errors you are making now should be acted on right away.
tiers.3: A hard deadline for the change shapes your schedule.
tiers.4: Using the available training makes practice count.
tiers.5: Encouraging others matters once your own adjustment is on track.

fact: The new system requires an extra field on every entry that the old way never asked for.
issues.action: Find out what the new field needs, and fill it in on every entry.
issues.brief: learn the new field and fill it in
issues.reason: A changed requirement applies to every entry from now on. Learning it now prevents a pile of incomplete records.
issues.lesson: When requirements change, learn the new expectation and apply it consistently.

shortcut.text: Leave the new field blank until someone explains why it matters.
shortcut.why: Blank required fields make records incomplete. You can find out what it needs now.
shortcut.mis: Requirements you do not understand can be ignored.

fact: {Lead|the} pointed out two errors you made in the new system yesterday.
clear: {Lead|the} already walked you through the right steps after yesterday's errors.
issues.done: {lead|the} already showed you the correct steps
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} to show you the correct steps, and practice them.
issues.brief: get shown the right steps and practice
issues.reason: Feedback only helps if you act on it. Learning the correct steps now stops the errors from repeating.
issues.lesson: Act on feedback quickly by learning and practicing the correction.

shortcut.text: Explain that the old way was easier and the errors were not your fault.
shortcut.why: Defending yourself does not prevent the errors from happening again.
shortcut.mis: Feedback is something to defend against.

fact: The old way ends on Friday, and you have not tried the new version yet.
clear: You practiced in the new version for an hour on Monday.
issues.done: you already practiced in the new version
issues.action: Schedule time this week to practice in the new version before Friday.
issues.reason: Practicing before the cutover lets you learn without the pressure of real work.
issues.lesson: Prepare for a change before it arrives, not after.

shortcut.text: Wait until Friday and learn it as you go.
shortcut.why: Learning under deadline pressure leads to errors and stress.

fact: Training videos and a help guide are posted, but you have not opened them.
issues.action: Work through the posted training before asking others for help.
issues.reason: The training answers most common questions. Using it first saves your coworkers' time.
issues.lesson: Use the learning resources available before relying on others.

shortcut.text: Ask {coworker} to walk you through everything from scratch.
shortcut.why: Asking for a full walkthrough ignores the training already posted and takes a coworker's time.
shortcut.mis: Asking someone is always faster than training materials.

fact: {coworker3} plans to keep using paper notes instead of the new version.
issues.action: Keep using the new version yourself and offer to share what you have learned.
issues.brief: keep using it and offer to share tips
issues.reason: Modeling the change and offering help supports a coworker without lecturing them.
issues.lesson: Adapt to change yourself and help others adapt.

shortcut.text: Join {coworker3} with paper notes until the new version improves.
shortcut.why: Avoiding the new version leaves records incomplete and delays your own learning.
shortcut.mis: If others resist a change, it is fine to resist too.

proceed.text: Keep entering {record|the} in the new version and build your speed.
proceed.why: You are prepared and on track, so regular use is the best way to become fluent.
proceed.lesson: Once you are prepared, regular practice makes a new system second nature.

generic.text: Complain to {lead|the} that the change was unnecessary.
generic.why: Complaining does not help you learn the system the team now uses.
generic.mis: Objecting to a change makes it go away.

generic.text: Keep a private paper copy of everything just in case.
generic.why: A separate copy creates two sets of records that may not match.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to approve each entry you make in the new version.
overcaution.why: You are prepared and on track. Approving every entry would waste the lead's time.
overcaution.mis: New systems need supervisor approval for every step.

setup: {Workplace|the} is switching {record|the} over to an updated {system}.

training: Training videos for the new version are available.
errors: You have already made a few errors in the new version.

steps.text: Enter real records in the updated system
Ask {lead|the} to spot-check your first entries

rel: Training shows you what to practice.
Correct your errors before entering real records.
Spot-checks happen after real entries are made.
process.lesson: Learn from the training, practice, fix your errors, then work for real and get checked.

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and just had your yearly review with {lead|the}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are thinking about what {lead|the} said in your review this week.
pressure: You feel a little discouraged after the review.
detail: Most of the review was positive.
The review took about half an hour.

tiers.1: A credential your job requires cannot be allowed to lapse.
tiers.2: Understand feedback before deciding what to do about it.
tiers.3: Specific feedback calls for a specific plan.
tiers.4: A skill gap for upcoming work needs a learning plan.
tiers.5: Checking your progress is useful once the work is underway.

fact: A certification your job requires expires next month, and renewal takes three weeks.
clear: You already signed up for the renewal course that starts Monday.
issues.action: Sign up for the renewal course now so the certification does not lapse.
issues.reason: If a required credential lapses, you may not be allowed to do your job. Renewal takes time, so it cannot wait.
issues.lesson: Keep required credentials current by renewing well before they expire.

shortcut.text: Renew it after it expires, since it is just paperwork.
shortcut.why: An expired required credential can keep you from working until it is renewed.
shortcut.mis: Credentials can be renewed whenever convenient.

fact: Part of the feedback felt unfair, and you are not sure what {lead|the} meant by it.
issues.short: the feedback you are unsure about
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} questions to understand that feedback before deciding what to do.
issues.reason: Feedback that feels unfair often makes more sense with an example. Understanding it first lets you respond well.
issues.lesson: Seek to understand feedback before reacting to it.

shortcut.text: Ignore that part of the review, since it felt unfair.
shortcut.why: Ignoring feedback you do not like may leave a real issue unaddressed.
shortcut.mis: Feedback that feels unfair is not worth considering.

fact: {Lead|the} said your written reports need clearer summaries.
issues.action: Ask for an example of a strong summary and practice that style.
issues.reason: An example shows exactly what clear looks like, and practice turns feedback into a habit.
issues.lesson: Turn specific feedback into a specific practice plan.

shortcut.text: Make your reports longer so nothing is left out.
shortcut.why: Longer is not clearer. The feedback was about summaries, not length.
shortcut.mis: More detail always means better writing.

fact: Next month you will take on a task that needs spreadsheet skills you do not have.
issues.action: Find a free online course or ask {coworker} to show you the basics before next month.
issues.brief: learn spreadsheet basics before next month
issues.reason: Learning before the task arrives lets you start strong instead of struggling.
issues.lesson: Identify the skills upcoming work requires and learn them ahead of time.

shortcut.text: Hope the task turns out simpler than expected.
shortcut.why: Hoping does not build the skill. You know the gap now and can close it.
shortcut.mis: Skill gaps solve themselves on the job.

clear: You finished a free spreadsheet course last month.
issues.done: you already learned the spreadsheet basics

fact: You have practiced a new skill for a month but have not checked whether it shows in your work.
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} whether the change is showing in your work.
issues.reason: Checking in confirms you are improving in the way that matters and shows you took the feedback seriously.
issues.lesson: Close the loop on feedback by checking whether your improvement shows.

shortcut.text: Assume it is fine, since {lead|the} has not said anything.
shortcut.why: Silence is not confirmation. A quick check gives you real information.

proceed.text: Keep working on the goals from your review and note your progress.
proceed.why: Nothing urgent needs handling, so steady work on the review goals is the right next step.
proceed.lesson: Make growth a steady habit after every review.

generic.text: Put the review in a drawer and forget about it until next year.
generic.why: A review only helps if you act on it during the year.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} to compare their review with yours.
generic.why: Comparing reviews does not help you act on your own feedback.
generic.mis: Your review only means something compared with others.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} for a second full review before doing anything.
overcaution.why: You already have clear feedback. A second review delays action.

title: Your learning plan after the review
intro: You wrote this learning plan after your review. Check it before sharing it with {lead|the}.
doc.lesson: A good learning plan responds to specific feedback with specific actions, resources and dates.

lines.text: Feedback: my report summaries need to be clearer.
Action: study two strong example summaries and rewrite mine in that style.
lines.fine: A specific action tied to the feedback.

bad.text: Action: take a course on public speaking.
bad.why: The feedback was about written summaries. A speaking course does not address it.

lines.text: Resource: ask {coworker} for examples; use the posted writing guide.
Certification renewal: course booked for next week, before it expires.

bad.text: Certification renewal: will deal with it after it expires.
bad.why: Letting a required credential lapse can stop you from working.

lines.text: Check-in: ask {lead|the} in six weeks whether summaries have improved.

bad.text: Check-in: none; I will assume it worked.
bad.why: Without checking, you cannot know whether the change is showing.

lines.text: I am glad to get specific feedback I can act on.

bad.text: I do not agree with the feedback, so this plan is mostly for show.
bad.why: A plan written only for show does not lead to improvement.

review.notes: Credential timing is stated in the scenario; no claims about specific licensing rules.
